title: Why I left Germany — and what it taught me about sovereignty
tweets:
In 2023 I took a trip to Southeast Asia and something broke in me.

Not in a bad way. In the way that happens when you realize the life you've been building doesn't actually belong to you. 🧵

I had a good job in Germany. Stable income, decent salary, all the markers of a reasonable adult life.

But I was living inside someone else's schedule, someone else's risk tolerance, someone else's definition of what the next ten years should look like.

I didn't choose any of it. I'd just kept moving forward because stopping felt harder than continuing.

Southeast Asia broke the spell.

Not because it was exotic or cheap or some digital nomad fantasy. But because I met people who had made a different calculation — who had decided that control over their own time was worth more than the security of the arrangement they'd been handed.

That calculation felt familiar. I'd seen it somewhere before.

Bitcoin asks the same question in a different domain:

Who actually controls this? Who can say no?

The answer for most people, when they trace it honestly, is: someone else. Their bank. Their employer. Their government. Their lease.

I moved to Bangkok in late 2025.

It was uncomfortable in ways I didn't expect. No safety net means no safety net. You feel it.

But the discomfort has a different quality than the slow discomfort of living inside arrangements you never consciously chose. One is the weight of responsibility. The other is the weight of dependence.

Self-sovereignty isn't a feeling. It's a series of decisions you make about what you're willing to own.

Your keys. Your time. Your location. Your choices.

None of it is free. All of it is yours.

I'm still figuring it out. But I'd rather figure it out than have it figured out for me.
